questions.question: What is the best FNP approach before initiating or escalating acid suppression for a patient with chest burning?
choices: Assume all burning is GERD
Assess for cardiac and GI alarm features as well as the reflux pattern
Start two acid-suppressing medications indefinitely
Avoid asking about medications
questions.explanation: Retrosternal burning can be GERD, but ischemia and other serious conditions can present atypically. Symptoms, risk factors, and alarm features guide safe disposition and treatment.

questions.question: What should be documented and periodically reassessed for a patient receiving long-term PPI therapy?
choices: Only the brand name
The ongoing indication, benefit, risk context, and whether step-down is appropriate
The patient’s favorite antacid
Nothing if the PPI is over the counter
questions.explanation: PPI therapy should have a documented indication and periodic review. Some patients need continued therapy; others may be candidates for supervised de-prescribing based on risk and indication.

questions.question: Which patient is least appropriate for an unstructured PPI discontinuation trial?
choices: A patient with a clear high-risk or complicated upper-GI indication
A patient whose transient reflux resolved and has no ongoing indication
A patient asking about timing of an antacid
A patient with a single episode of mild heartburn
questions.explanation: Complicated erosive disease, Barrett’s esophagus, high upper-GI bleeding risk, and other specific contexts may warrant continued therapy. De-prescribing is individualized.

questions.question: Why is medication reconciliation important in a patient with dyspepsia or GI bleeding risk?
choices: NSAIDs, anticoagulants, corticosteroids, and OTC products can alter mucosal and bleeding risk
OTC medications never affect the GI tract
It replaces a history and examination
It is relevant only in pediatrics
questions.explanation: NSAIDs and other medications can increase ulcer or bleeding risk, and multiple OTC products may be missed unless specifically reviewed.

questions.question: Which factor most increases concern when considering an antiemetic for a patient with vomiting?
choices: The patient asks for a refill
Electrolyte loss plus concurrent QT-prolonging medications
A normal hydration status
A preference for a tablet rather than liquid
questions.explanation: Vomiting can cause potassium and magnesium loss. Combined with QT-active medications or other risk factors, this can increase arrhythmia risk and may require evaluation before symptomatic treatment.

questions.question: Which finding with constipation requires urgent evaluation rather than routine laxative escalation?
choices: Mild constipation after reduced fiber intake
Progressive distention, vomiting, and inability to pass flatus
A request for more water intake advice
A stable chronic bowel pattern
questions.explanation: Distention, vomiting, and obstipation can indicate obstruction, ileus, impaction, or another urgent condition. Do not treat it as routine constipation.

questions.question: Which statement about polyethylene glycol (PEG) in chronic idiopathic constipation is most accurate?
choices: It is a medication option for appropriate patients after assessment for secondary or dangerous causes
It is appropriate when bowel obstruction is suspected
It replaces evaluation of new alarm features
It is an antiemetic
questions.explanation: PEG can be an appropriate medication option for chronic idiopathic constipation, but clinicians must first evaluate red flags, medication causes, hydration, and possible obstruction.

questions.question: What is the safest initial priority in significant acute diarrhea?
choices: Suppress all bowel movement immediately
Assess volume status, cause, and red flags while supporting hydration
Start antibiotics for every patient
Assume IBS
questions.explanation: Diarrhea management starts with hydration, severity assessment, and evaluation for infectious, inflammatory, ischemic, medication-related, and other causes.

questions.question: Why should antimotility medication not be used casually in diarrhea with fever, bloody stool, or severe abdominal pain?
choices: It always cures infection
The presentation may represent invasive or inflammatory disease needing evaluation
It improves dehydration instantly
It is required in every antibiotic-associated diarrhea case
questions.explanation: Fever, blood in stool, severe pain, or systemic illness can signal invasive, inflammatory, or other serious disease. Management must address cause and urgency before suppressing motility.

questions.question: A patient requests a stronger PPI but has progressive dysphagia and unintentional weight loss. What is the priority?
choices: Routine refill without follow-up
Recognize alarm features and arrange prompt diagnostic evaluation/referral
Add an antimotility agent
Assume symptoms are functional
questions.explanation: Progressive dysphagia and unintentional weight loss are alarm features. Acid suppression must not delay appropriate investigation and referral.
